title: Cairo founded
hook: the Fatimids, an Isma'ili dynasty, found a new city beside the Nile

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fatimah al-Fihri, who built a mosque in Fez with her inheritance, and a university grew inside it. Your line was: she founded a university. Whose name did you pass on? Day nine hundred forty-six.

Ropes are strung around a plain beside the Nile, hung with bells. Workers wait with their tools. Astrologers watch the sky for the right moment to begin, and when it comes, they'll shake the ropes and the digging will start. Then a crow lands on a rope. The bells ring. The workers dig. And the planet rising at that moment, so the story goes, was the one Arabic astronomers called the victorious. That, people say, is how the city got its name: al-Qahira. In English, Cairo.

Take the crow as a story people tell; the history behind it is sturdier. Start with the name of the dynasty. The Fatimids named themselves for Fatimah, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and wife of Ali, and they claimed descent from her. They were Isma'ili Shi'i Muslims. Shi'i Muslims hold that leadership of the community passed to Ali, and then to imams among his and Fatimah's descendants. The Isma'ilis followed one line of those imams, and the Fatimid caliphs said they were those imams. That made for a crowded sky of caliphs: one in Baghdad, a Fatimid caliph who had already claimed the title in North Africa, and the Cordoba caliph you met last week, who took it after them. Each claimed to lead. Sunnis and Shi'is understood that leadership differently, and still do. The Fatimids rose in North Africa, then took Egypt. Their general, Jawhar, laid out a new walled city for his caliph, al-Mu'izz. It wasn't alone. An older city, Fustat, already stood nearby, built in the early years of Muslim rule in Egypt. The new city was a royal enclosure: palaces, a great mosque, walls with gates. Much of ordinary life went on outside it, in Fustat. Over the years, the royal city and the old one grew into each other, until the name Cairo covered them both. Today Isma'ili Muslims, in communities around the world, count the Fatimid imams as part of their own story, and Cairo still keeps Fatimid gates and mosques among its streets. A city built to announce a claim, and then lived in by everyone. The victorious city.
screen: `A DYNASTY NAMED FOR FATIMAH.` · `ISMA'ILI IMAMS, A RIVAL CALIPH.` · `A ROYAL CITY BESIDE FUSTAT.` · `THE CITIES GROW INTO ONE.` · then, large: `THE VICTORIOUS CITY.`

segments.voice: The practice: get ready to look at a map of Cairo. Settle, and breathe. Picture the Nile running north, a wide brown ribbon. On its east bank, two cities: an old, busy one, and a new walled one with palaces, side by side, slowly merging. Now picture your own town the same way. Where was the old center? Where did newer neighborhoods grow, and who lives in them? Let the map of your own place come into focus. If you pray, you can remember the people of your city in your prayer. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with good will. The bell holds the time.
Cairo founded. The Fatimids, an Isma'ili dynasty, built a royal city beside the old Fustat, and named it al-Qahira, the victorious. Today's word.
Your line: the victorious city. Today, open a map of Cairo, find the Nile, and see if you can spot the old Fatimid gates on the east bank. Day nine hundred forty-six.

howItsDone: Isma'ili Muslims today count the Fatimid imams as part of their own history, and Cairo's Fatimid gates and mosques are still visited and prayed in.

fork.setup: you're a worker beside the Nile. ropes with bells circle the plain, and the astrologers are still waiting for the right moment. a crow lands on a rope. what happens?
options: the bells ring, and the digging starts early.
fork.reveal: in the story people tell, the bells ring and the digging begins, under the planet called the victorious, and the city takes the name al-Qahira.

original.note: Arabic: al-Qahira, Cairo's name, usually given as the victorious.

trapdoor: what you thought: an ancient city that was always there.
what it means: a royal city laid out by the Fatimids beside the older Fustat, which grew into one Cairo.
what a scholar hears: an Isma'ili caliphate's capital, built by Jawhar for al-Mu'izz, with a legend of a crow, bells and a victorious planet.

notes: The founding date in the index hook is left out under the claims rule; the hook field is rewritten without it.
The bells-and-crow legend and the planet (Mars, al-Qahir) are told as 'a story people tell'; confirm the legend's details as given in al-Maqrizi.
'al-Qahira, the victorious' is the index carry; the name's meaning is given as 'usually given as' in the original-game note. Confirm.
Isma'ili and Shi'i beliefs are summarized briefly; an Isma'ili and a Sunni reviewer should both confirm the description is fair. 'Much of ordinary life went on outside it' should be confirmed or cut.
Fustat described as 'built in the early years of Muslim rule in Egypt' (Amr ibn al-As); confirm.

Audit: corrected the order of the caliphates. The teach had the Fatimid caliph arriving 'now', after Cordoba's; the Fatimids proclaimed their caliphate in North Africa (909) before Abd al-Rahman III took the title (929). Dates are kept out of the voice. Also tightened the Shi'i summary to 'passed to Ali, and then to imams among his and Fatimah's descendants'.
